spec_choices.why: The designer fixed the table at 3, and the deal (six permutations of three compositions) only works for 3 seats.

spec_choices.what: Tie-break encoded as key = bid*3 + ((3 - offset) mod 3), where offset = (seat - auctioneer + 3) mod 3
spec_choices.why: This turns the seat-order tie rule into arithmetic: the seat after the auctioneer has priority 2, the next has 1, and the auctioneer has 0. All-zero bids are a separate case that gives the painting to the auctioneer.

spec_choices.what: Talk kept as a simultaneous poll broadcast to all, before the bid poll
spec_choices.why: The source requires it. It also earns its place: players disagree about which artist to push and can bluff about their hidden compositions.

spec_choices.what: Helper table attributes season_ended, scoring_now, winner_seat, price, first_artist and second_artist
spec_choices.why: The flat step list needs flags so that later steps can carry arithmetic 'when' conditions.

spec_choices.what: If no seat has cards when the role passes, the auctioneer is left unchanged
spec_choices.why: The game ends at the check in the same round, so the value never matters.

A thoughtful player infers the others' compositions from what they play and bid, steers seasons toward artists they own, bids up to an artist's likely payout, and sometimes buys their own card so it scores for them.

simplifications.what: A tie for the most money is reported as a shared win among the tied players, not as a separate draw
simplifications.why: The engine ranks by one expression and players level at the top share the win, which corresponds to the source's draw.

simplifications.what: The hand is three counters (hand_red, hand_blue, hand_green) rather than a list of cards
simplifications.why: Cards of one artist are identical, so counts carry exactly the same information.

variation.original_summary: Modern Art is a 3-5 player auction game. Players auction paintings by five artists using five auction types. At the end of each of four rounds the most-played artists gain value, and the paintings players own of those artists pay out. Most money wins.

review.evidence: No simple policy wins. Never bidding leaves you with only the paintings you auction and keep, so you cash few placed paintings. Always bidding highest overpays and transfers money to rivals. Market value depends on which artists the table pushes. Seat order matters slightly, but the auction role rotates.

Valuing a painting before an artist's ranking is known, and timing which cards to play, are well-known skill differentiators. The random deal matters, but a skilled player outbids, undersells and steers rankings over 4 rounds.
Valuation is never solved, because it depends on rivals' hidden hands and intentions. A weak player still earns money by selling paintings, so scores are never zero.
Hands and money are hidden. A player must infer which artists rivals hold from what they auction and bid on, predict the ranking, and plan several rounds ahead because values accumulate.
Rankings, payouts and money totals are pure arithmetic.

It has five auction types, two of them sequential and open (open ascending is near real-time). It has a physical value board, five artists with ranking ties, a deal of 40+ random cards, and up to about 70 auctions. The previous variation left reveals undefined and understated its draws, steps and attributes.

problems: Five auction types (open ascending, once-around, fixed price, double) need sequential or near-real-time bidding and many steps; only sealed simultaneous bidding fits cheaply.
Dealing dozens of random cards one at a time breaks the limit of 1 random draw per round and costs many remove/append steps (previous variation: 30+ draws declared as 0).
Ranking 4-5 artists with tie-breaks, and paying every player for every artist, exceeds the step and attribute budget (previous variation understated both).
The previous variation never said what is announced after an auction (bids, winner, price, reserve), nor whether money and owned paintings are public, so players cannot track rivals.
The previous variation did not state that a painting the auctioneer keeps joins their owned paintings and scores.
The secret reserve added a fourth hidden element and an extra choice step for little strategic gain.
Full game length (4 rounds, about 70 auctions) is too long for the platform.

changes.what: Use one auction type: a simultaneous sealed bid in which the auctioneer also bids. If the auctioneer is highest, they pay the bank; if every bid is 0, the auctioneer keeps the painting for free.
changes.why: This keeps Modern Art's 'buy your own painting from the bank' tension. It needs only one simultaneous poll and replaces the secret reserve.
changes.fixes: Five auction types (open ascending, once-around, fixed price, double) need sequential or near-real-time bidding and many steps; only sealed simultaneous bidding fits cheaply.

changes.what: Replace the card deal with three fixed 7-card hand compositions, each strong in one artist. One random draw at setup (a number 1-6) assigns the compositions to the seats through a fixed table.
changes.why: This takes exactly one random draw and one assignment step. The compositions are rotations of each other, so the deal is balanced. A player's composition is a hidden type that rivals must infer from what they auction and bid on.
changes.fixes: Dealing dozens of random cards one at a time breaks the limit of 1 random draw per round and costs many remove/append steps (previous variation: 30+ draws declared as 0).

changes.what: Cut to 3 artists and 3 players. Only the top two artists place, earning +20 and +10. The ranking uses a fixed tie order (Red, Blue, Green). The payout is one formula per player: owned count times cumulative value, summed over placed artists. Owned paintings are tracked as per-player counts for each artist.
changes.why: The ranking takes 2 calc steps and the payout 1 step, so the game fits 20 attributes and 20 steps when counted honestly.
changes.fixes: Ranking 4-5 artists with tie-breaks, and paying every player for every artist, exceeds the step and attribute budget (previous variation understated both).

changes.what: After every auction, announce all bids, the buyer and the price. Money and owned paintings are public. Only hand contents are hidden. The card played is always announced.
changes.why: Every player has the same public record to reason from. The hidden information is concentrated in hands, as in the original.
changes.fixes: The previous variation never said what is announced after an auction (bids, winner, price, reserve), nor whether money and owned paintings are public, so players cannot track rivals.

changes.what: State explicitly that every painting the auctioneer keeps (bought from the bank or taken for free) is added to the auctioneer's owned count for that artist and scores normally.
changes.why: This removes the ambiguity about whether kept paintings score.
changes.fixes: The previous variation did not state that a painting the auctioneer keeps joins their owned paintings and scores.

changes.why: The auctioneer's own sealed bid serves the same purpose. This leaves 2 hidden elements (hands and sealed bids) and 3 choice steps.
changes.fixes: The secret reserve added a fourth hidden element and an extra choice step for little strategic gain.

changes.what: Play 3 seasons. A season ends when the third card of one artist is played; that card is unsold. The game lasts at most 21 rounds, one card per round.
changes.why: The game stays short while keeping cumulative artist values across seasons.
changes.fixes: Full game length (4 rounds, about 70 auctions) is too long for the platform.

keeps: Players auction paintings from a hidden hand, and the auctioneer earns the sale price.
The auctioneer may buy their own painting by paying the bank.
The season ends when one artist reaches a card limit, and that final card goes unsold.
Artists are ranked by cards played in the season, and the top artists gain value.
Values accumulate across seasons, so a repeat winner becomes very valuable.
Owned paintings pay out only if their artist placed this season, then are discarded.

recommendation.reason: Its core (valuing paintings whose worth depends on hidden hands and on rivals' play, then steering the ranking) survives as a 3-artist sealed-bid game within the limits.

variation.name: Modern Art: Three Studios
variation.summary: Three players each hold a hidden 7-card hand strong in one of three artists. Each round one player auctions a card by simultaneous sealed bid, in which the auctioneer also bids. Seasons end when an artist's third card appears. The top two artists gain cumulative value, and owned paintings of those artists pay out. Most money after 3 seasons wins.
variation.rules:
R1 Setup. There are 3 players in seats 1, 2 and 3, and 3 artists: Red, Blue and Green. Each player starts with 60 money. Money is public at all times. Each player has hand counts for Red, Blue and Green and owned counts for Red, Blue and Green; all owned counts start at 0. On the table, each artist has a season count and a cumulative value, all starting at 0. seasons_done starts at 0 and the auctioneer is seat 1.

R2 Hands, at setup only. There are three hand compositions of 7 cards each. Composition A is 4 Red, 2 Blue, 1 Green. Composition B is 1 Red, 4 Blue, 2 Green. Composition C is 2 Red, 1 Blue, 4 Green. The engine draws one random whole number from 1 to 6 and gives compositions to seats 1, 2 and 3 as follows: 1 gives A,B,C; 2 gives A,C,B; 3 gives B,A,C; 4 gives B,C,A; 5 gives C,A,B; 6 gives C,B,A. Each player sees only their own hand counts. Everyone knows the three compositions exist and that each player has a different one. This is the only random event in the game.

R3 Choose a card. The auctioneer chooses one artist from those for which their hand count is above 0.

R4 Reveal. The chosen artist is announced to everyone as the current artist. The auctioneer's hand count for that artist falls by 1, and that artist's season count rises by 1.

R5 Season-ending card. If the current artist's season count is now 3, the card is discarded unsold. Skip R6 to R8 this round and go to R9.

R6 Talk. Otherwise, all three players each write one short message at the same moment without seeing the others. All messages are then shown to everyone. Talk is not binding.

R7 Sealed bids. Otherwise, all three players, the auctioneer included, submit at the same moment a whole-number bid from 0 up to their current money. The highest bid wins. If bids tie for highest, the tied player who comes first in seat order starting from the seat after the auctioneer wins, with the auctioneer last. If every bid is 0, the auctioneer wins at price 0.

R8 Settle and announce. If the winner is not the auctioneer, the winner pays their bid to the auctioneer. If the winner is the auctioneer, they pay their bid to the bank (nothing if it is 0). In every case the winner's owned count for the current artist rises by 1; this includes paintings the auctioneer keeps, which score like any other. All three bids, the winner and the price are announced to everyone. Owned counts are public.

R9 Season scoring. Scoring happens if the season-ending card was just played (R5), or if all hands are now empty and at least one season count is above 0. When it happens:
(a) First place is the artist with the highest season count, ties broken in the order Red, Blue, Green. Its cumulative value rises by 20.
(b) Second place is the highest of the remaining two artists by season count, same tie order, but only if its season count is above 0. Its cumulative value rises by 10.
(c) The third artist, and any artist with season count 0, does not place.
(d) Each player receives from the bank, for each placed artist, their owned count of that artist times that artist's cumulative value. Unplaced artists pay 0. Note that a cumulative value can be above 0 from earlier seasons, but it pays only if the artist placed this season.
(e) The placings, the new cumulative values and each player's payout are announced.
(f) All owned counts reset to 0, all season counts reset to 0, and seasons_done rises by 1.

R10 Pass the role. The auctioneer role passes to the next seat (1 to 2, 2 to 3, 3 to 1). It skips any seat whose hand is empty.

R11 End. The game ends when seasons_done reaches 3, or when all hands are empty (after R9 has scored any unfinished season). The game lasts at most 21 rounds.
variation.objective: When the game ends, the player with the most money wins. If two or three players tie for the most money, the game is a draw.
variation.expected_effect: Each player wants their own strong artist to place, because they can supply it and buy it cheaply, and rivals' strong artists to fail. Bids therefore signal private information. Heavy bidding on Blue hints that you hold Blue or expect it to place, and the cards a player auctions reveal their composition. Players must infer rivals' compositions, value paintings before the ranking is known, and judge when to buy their own painting from the bank to keep a painting rather than sell it cheaply. Bidding 0 always only earns sale revenue and loses to profitable buyers; maximum bidding overpays and loses. Talk passes both tests: players disagree over prices (seller against buyers) and over which artist should place (each prefers their own strong one). A player who follows a rival's claim that 'Green will place' can buy Green, watch the rival play Red instead, and be left with worthless paintings. The deal is symmetric by rotation, so the hidden type changes what to do, not who is ahead. Seat 1 may auction one more time if the game ends at 3 seasons; the random seat assignment of compositions limits this.

balanced.evidence: VALUES: a painting pays its artist's cumulative value only if the artist places in that season. Season 1 values are 30/20/10. The most an artist can reach is 90 (first in all three seasons). So the ceiling per painting is 30 in season 1, 60 in season 2 and 90 in season 3. Starting money is 100. THOUGHTLESS POLICIES, judged by the winner rule: (a) ALWAYS BID ALL MONEY. It wins almost every painting it bids on, but pays about 100, then 100 plus income, for an item worth at most 30, 60 or 90. Net is about -70 per season-1 purchase, and it is nearly broke after one buy. It loses to sensible play and to random play. (b) ALWAYS BID 0. It keeps 100 plus its own sale income and earns no buyer surplus. Against random bidders (uniform 0..money, mean about 50 against a value of at most 30 early) the random players burn money, so this policy beats random. Against sensible bidders who buy below value, they gain surplus on top of the same kind of sale income, so it loses narrowly but regularly. It does not avoid losing, so it is not dominant. (c) ALWAYS RESERVE 0 AND PLAY THE FIRST CARD. Sensible bidders take the paintings cheaply, and the policy cannot steer which artist places. It loses to sensible auctioneers. (d) ALWAYS RESERVE = ALL MONEY. Bidders rarely meet it, so it pays its whole stack to the bank for one painting. Big loss. No option is strictly better whatever others do. The bid trade-off is sealed first-price shading against competition. The reserve trade-off is protection against the risk of paying the bank. SEATS: the auctioneer role rotates and each seat auctions about equally (10 or 8 cards). Seat 1 may get one extra auction if seasons end early. That is a small edge, partly offset because any auctioneer can be forced into a dead season-ending round. The bid tie-break favours the seat after the auctioneer, and it rotates, so it is neutral overall. Ranking tie-breaks favour red, which has the fewest cards (10 against yellow's 13). Fewer cards but tie priority is a reasonable counterweight. Every player can realistically win.

playable.evidence: GAPS: (1) R7 never says whether the winning bid, the winner's identity, or the losing bids are announced. Money is 'visible only to its owner', so it is undefined what others learn. Models cannot track rivals' paintings or cash without this. (2) It is not stated whether owned paintings are public. Opponent modelling at scoring depends on it. (3) 'The auctioneer keeps the painting' does not explicitly add it to the auctioneer's owned paintings, so it is unclear whether it scores. LIMITS: (4) R2 deals 30 or 32 individual random draws. random_draws_per_round is at most 1, yet the designer declares 0, which hides the cost. Drawing is a remove/append workaround, so 30+ draws cost many steps. (5) R8 needs ranking with tie-breaks (arithmetic_ranking needs calc), +30/+20/+10, and a payout for each player for each artist. With per-player owned counts for 4 artists, plus money, hand, 4 season counts, 4 cumulative values, seasons_done, current_artist, auctioneer, reserve and bids, the claimed 15 attributes and 14 steps look understated. It plausibly exceeds 20 steps on a scoring round. Sealed bids plus reserve, money and hands may also make 4 hidden elements, not 3. WHAT WORKS: the game is finite (one card per round, cap = total hand cards: 30 or 32), and R5's single-step `when` skips are fine. Talk is simultaneous and placed where interests conflict: bidders vs auctioneer over price, and pushing artists to place. That is a sensible inclusion.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence: Chance comes only from the initial deal. With 10 or 8 cards from 4 near-even colours (10/11/12/13), hands are fairly balanced. Decisions dominate. Players must value paintings by predicting which artists will place, inferring rivals' hands from played cards and from the 16 or 14 unseen leftovers. They must shade sealed bids against 2-3 rivals, set reserves to deter lowballing, and time season-ending cards to dump a season (or deny one). When all play well, the winner is decided by valuation and timing, not by the deal alone. A strong deal (many cards of a likely leader) helps, but good bidding can buy into that artist. Estimated chance share is about 20-30%.

required_changes: State in R7 what is revealed after bidding: at minimum the winner and the price paid (or all bids), and the reserve. State whether owned paintings are public.
State in R7 that when no bid meets the reserve the painting goes into the auctioneer's owned paintings and scores like any other.

Replace the 30/32-draw deal with something inside the limits. Either use one setup shuffle and deal fixed consecutive slices, or give each player a fixed pre-listed hand composition with random order. Declare the true random-draw count.

Recount the complexity honestly, including per-player owned counts for 4 artists, the bids hidden element, and the calc steps for R8 ranking and payouts. If the scoring round exceeds 20 steps or 20 attributes, simplify, for example by tracking only a per-player 'owned value' accumulator updated at purchase, plus a fixed-table ranking.

balanced.evidence:
Symmetry: the compositions are cyclic shifts (A = 4R/2B/1G, B = 1R/4B/2G, C = 2R/1B/4G). Each artist has 7 cards in total. Each player holds a 4-2-1 split. The only asymmetries are the Red>Blue>Green tie order, which mildly favours the A holder in second-place ties, and seat 1 auctioning first.

Seat edge: total rounds n run from 9 to 21. Seat 1 auctions ceil(n/3) times, so at most one extra auction. The extra auction may be a season-ending card worth 0. Players can steer timing by their card choices, so the edge is small and not decisive.

Season values: each artist sells at most 2 cards per season, because its 3rd card ends the season unsold. A season pays at most 2 x first-place value plus 2 x second-place value. In season 1 that is 2x20 + 2x10 = 60 of new bank money.

Single-auction table (card worth V to all, sealed bids b_A for the auctioneer, b_X and b_Y for the others):
- X wins at b_X: X nets V - b_X, auctioneer nets +b_X.
- Auctioneer wins at b_A: auctioneer nets V - b_A (paid to the bank).
- All bid 0: auctioneer nets V.

Thoughtless policies, using the winner rule:
(1) Always bid 0. This player never collects bank payouts and earns only sale prices on its own auctions, about 1/3 of the turns. Sensible opponents bid 1 on its cards and compete with each other at prices below V. They gain surplus plus the bank injection, so the always-0 player ends lowest in most games. It can lose, so it fails as a dominant policy.
(2) Always bid all money. It pays up to 60 for a card worth at most 20 in season 1 and goes broke. It loses.
(3) Auctioneer always plays the first available artist (Red), or always its 4-card artist. Opponents read this and bid accordingly, and the season ender is predictable. It does not win reliably.
(4) Random bidding. It overpays or underbids at random against sensible play and loses most games.

No bid or card choice is strictly better regardless of opponents: the value of a card depends on which artist the other players push. All three seats can win. Ties for most money are possible but rare with integer money, and they are a draw.

playable.evidence:
Rules cover every case:
- Choosing a card is limited to non-empty hand counts.
- The season ender is discarded, with explicit skips.
- The sealed-bid tie-break rotates from the seat after the auctioneer, with the all-zero case overridden explicitly.
- Payment goes to the auctioneer, or to the bank if the auctioneer wins.
- First and second place have explicit tie orders, and a count-0 artist cannot place.
- Payouts use cumulative value only for artists placed this season.
- Owned and season counts reset each season.
- The role passes and skips empty hands.
- The game ends at 3 seasons or when hands are empty, after a final scoring.

The game is finite (at most 21 rounds) and decided by arithmetic on public money.

Skipping R6 to R8 is done by per-step `when` conditions, not by choosing between blocks, so it is supported.

Limits: steps 17 of 20; choice steps 3 of 4 (card, talk, bid); attributes 20 of 20, at the cap (about 8 per-player and 12 table attributes); hidden elements 2 of 3 (hands, sealed bids); one random draw at setup only; rounds 21 of 40. No board, clock, trading or binding agreement is needed.

Talk is justified. Interests conflict: the auctioneer wants high prices, buyers want low ones, and players disagree about which artist to push. Talk is simultaneous and placed before the sealed bids, where bluffing about holdings and price signalling can cost a player who follows it.

This is not a fixed-length cooperation dilemma, so the 'safe late option' failure does not apply.

design_flags_left: always taking the first option as seat 1 wins 98% of decided matches against random seats
always taking the first option as seat 2 wins 98% of decided matches against random seats

triage.reason: The tests match the rules: the auctioneer must pick a reserve from 0 up to their current money. The game never put 0, 25 or 100 to seat 1 as a reserve option, so the reserve fell back to a default and the table `reserve` stayed 0 when it should have been 25. The reserve choice step is missing or wrongly built in the game file; the rules themselves are fine.
triage.guidance: Make the auctioneer's reserve choice a real offered choice. It should be a numeric choice or an option list covering every whole number from `min_reserve` (0) up to that auctioneer's current `money` inclusive, so 0, 25 and 100 are all offered when money is 100. Take the bounds from the parameter attribute and the player's money, not from hard-coded numbers. After the season-end check, when the season does not end, copy the chosen reserve into the table `reserve` so it is announced (for example 25 when 25 is chosen). Keep the card choice limited to the cards in the auctioneer's hand, which already works. Check that both choices are only for the auctioneer seat, and that the reserve is ignored and bidding skipped when the revealed card brings the count to `season_end_count`. Also check that the bidders' bids are offered the same way, from `min_bid` up to each bidder's own money.

triage.reason: The reserve choice is not built correctly. Seat 1 was never offered a reserve of 0 or 100, and an auctioneer choosing 25 still left the table `reserve` at 0. The card choice worked, so the fault is in the reserve step, not in the rules or the tests.
triage.guidance:
1. Make the auctioneer's reserve a real choice put to the auctioneer seat only, offering every whole number from `min_reserve` (0) up to that seat's current `money` inclusive, so 0 and 100 are both offered at 100 money. Use a parameter attribute for the minimum, not a literal.
2. After the choice, copy the chosen reserve into the table `reserve` in the not-season-ending branch, guarded with `when`/`if` on the season-end check, so it is announced. Do not leave `reserve` at its default 0.
3. Make sure the card choice and the reserve choice are two separate prompts to the auctioneer in that order.
4. Increment the matching `count_*` from the chosen card and remove that card from the auctioneer's hand.
5. When the season count reaches `season_end_count`, skip talk and bidding and go straight to scoring.
6. When a scenario supplies starting hands, do not deal over them, so the given hands are used as given.

triage.reason: The rules are clear and within the platform's capabilities, but the file deals 9 cards each instead of 10. Its trace shows some 'pick' draws (e.g. green) that never reach a hand, so the deal loop loses picks. The R3 to R5 scenarios also show the reserve choice is never put to the auctioneer as options from 0 to their current money.
triage.guidance: Rewrite the deal so every draw lands. Repeat exactly hand_size times per player, where hand_size is hand_size_3_players or hand_size_4_players depending on player count. On each repetition, take a random card from the deck list, remove that card from the deck and append it to the player's hand. Do not pick an artist name from a separate offer list, which can fail to match a deck card and waste the draw. Afterwards the deck must hold deck_size minus hand_size × players cards (16 with 3 players, 14 with 4). For the round, offer the auctioneer two choices. The first is a card choice whose options are exactly the cards in their hand. The second is a reserve choice whose options are every whole number from min_reserve (0) up to their current money (so 100 is offered at the start). Then remove the chosen card from the hand, set current_artist, and add 1 to that artist's count. If the count reaches season_end_count, skip talk and bidding by putting `when` conditions on those steps, and run season scoring.

triage.reason: The trace shows the file departing from the rules. Seat 1's dealt hand was overwritten after the deal: on roll 6 it got C (2,1,4), then hand_blue went 1->2 and hand_green 4->2. The bid and choice steps also do not offer what R3 and R7 require: no seat was ever offered a bid of 0 or 10, and seat 1 played Green although its rule asked for Red.
triage.guidance: 1) Deal (R2): apply exactly one composition per seat for the drawn roll, using parameter attributes. Make the six roll branches mutually exclusive with `when`/`if` conditions so no later step overwrites an earlier assignment. For roll 6 the hands must be seat 1 = C (2,1,4), seat 2 = B (1,4,2), seat 3 = A (4,2,1), and nothing may change them before the first play. 2) Choose a card (R3): build the auctioneer's offer from only the artists with hand count above 0, at the moment of the choice. Present it as the option list the auctioneer actually chooses from, so Red, Blue or Green are real selectable options. 3) Bids (R7): put a simultaneous numeric bid to all three seats, the auctioneer included, with options running from min_bid (0) to that seat's current money, so 0, 10 and every whole number up to money appear as options. 4) Leave current_artist as '' until the first card is revealed; do not set 'none yet'. 5) Check that the tie-break, the all-zero bid case (auctioneer wins at 0), settlement to the auctioneer or the bank, and R9 scoring use the interface attributes and parameters, not literal numbers.

triage.reason: The trace shows the game mishandling hands: after seat 1 played Green, its hand_blue rose from 1 to 2 and hand_green fell from 4 to 2, which breaks R4 (only the chosen artist's count falls, by 1). The bid step also never presents the 0 to money range in a way the tests recognise, so the seats were never offered 0 or 10 as bids.
triage.guidance:
1. Fix R4 so that playing artist X decrements only hand_X by 1 and increments only season_X by 1. Make sure no other hand attribute is written. The deal for roll 6 (C,B,A) should leave seat 1 with Red 2, Blue 1, Green 4, and after playing Green it should hold 2, 1, 3. Check every deal-table branch and the per-artist decrement steps for crossed attribute names or doubled operations.
2. Build the R3 offer from the auctioneer's own hand: include only artists whose hand count is above 0, recomputed each round. Offer it only to the auctioneer seat.
3. Make the talk step (R6) and the bid step (R7) simultaneous polls of all three seats, auctioneer included, and gate both with a `when` on the card not being season-ending.
4. Make the bid a numeric choice whose allowed values run from the min_bid attribute (0) up to that player's current money, so 0 and every whole number up to money are actually offered to each seat.
5. Then apply R7/R8: the tie-break starts from the seat after the auctioneer, with the auctioneer last. If all bids are 0, the auctioneer wins at 0. Payment goes to the auctioneer, or to the bank when the auctioneer wins. Set winner_seat and price, and increment the winner's owned count.

triage.reason: The tests' expectations follow R2, R3 and R7. The game never offered the sealed bids as options from 0 up to each bidder's money, so the bid rules 'never matched' for any seat. The deal is also corrupted: seat 1 was dealt C (2/1/4) and then its hand_blue went 1 -> 2, ending at 2/2/1 after one Green play.
triage.guidance: 1) Make the bid step (R7) a simultaneous numeric choice for all three seats, auctioneer included. Each seat must actually be offered every whole number from min_bid (0) up to its own current `money`, so 0 and 10 appear for a seat holding 60. Do not reuse the artist `offer` list for bids, and do not leave the bid range empty. 2) Fix the deal (R2). Exactly one branch must apply for the drawn deal_roll: each `when`/`if` must test that roll value alone, and later branches must not overwrite or add to hands. Use set operations, not additions. For roll 6, seat 1 must end with C (Red 2, Blue 1, Green 4) and keep it. 3) Build the artist choice (R3) from the auctioneer's own hand counts above 0, and decrement only that seat's hand for the chosen artist (R4). 4) Keep the tie-break and settlement as specified: seat order starting after the auctioneer, with the auctioneer last. If all bids are 0, the auctioneer wins at 0. An auctioneer who wins pays the bank.
